definition.text: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.

anchor.quote: convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose

facts.text: The light-dependent reactions produce ATP and NADPH from sunlight.

anchor.quote: The light-dependent reactions capture energy from sunlight to produce ATP and NADPH

facts.text: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar.

anchor.quote: the Calvin cycle then uses to fix carbon dioxide into sugar

facts.text: Oxygen is released as a byproduct of splitting water molecules.

anchor.quote: Oxygen is released as a byproduct of splitting water molecules

misconceptions.text: Students think plants get their mass mainly from soil rather than from carbon dioxide fixed during photosynthesis.

examples.text: A tree builds most of its woody mass from carbon captured out of the air.

mcBank.stem: During photosynthesis, the oxygen released by a plant comes from
options: water molecules that are split
carbon dioxide molecules
glucose breakdown
soil minerals

definition.text: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable barrier that regulates which substances enter and leave the cell.

anchor.quote: a selectively permeable barrier that regulates which substances enter and leave the cell

facts.text: The membrane is composed of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.

anchor.quote: composed of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins

facts.text: The membrane maintains the internal environment while allowing exchange of nutrients and wastes.

anchor.quote: maintains the internal environment of the cell while allowing the exchange of nutrients and wastes

misconceptions.text: Students think the membrane is a solid wall rather than a fluid, selectively permeable bilayer.

examples.text: Oxygen diffuses freely across the membrane while large charged ions require protein channels.

mcBank.stem: The cell membrane is best described as
options: selectively permeable
completely impermeable
freely permeable to everything
a rigid outer wall

mapping.what crosses: nutrients and wastes that the membrane regulates
mapping.what is excluded: large charged ions that cannot cross without protein channels

definition.text: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes in external conditions, usually through negative feedback.

anchor.quote: the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes in external conditions

facts.text: In negative feedback, a change in a regulated variable triggers a response that counteracts the change and returns it toward the set point.

anchor.quote: a change in a regulated variable triggers a response that counteracts the change and returns the variable toward its set point

facts.text: Sensors detect the deviation, a control center compares it to the set point, and effectors produce the corrective response.

anchor.quote: Sensors detect the deviation, a control center compares it to the set point, and effectors produce a corrective response

misconceptions.text: Students think homeostasis means an unchanging internal state, when it means a variable held near a set point by ongoing correction.
misconceptions.corrective: Homeostasis is active regulation around a set point, not a frozen constant.

examples.text: When body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation bring it back toward the set point.

mcBank.stem: In negative feedback regulation of body temperature, a rise above the set point triggers a response that
options: counteracts the rise and lowers temperature
amplifies the rise further
raises the set point permanently
removes the sensors from the loop

mapping.output signal: a deviation of a regulated variable from its set point
mapping.feedback path: sensors and the control center that detect and compare the deviation
mapping.effect on input: effectors that counteract the deviation and restore the set point

definition.text: Optimal foraging theory models an animal as maximizing its net energy gain subject to the constraints of time and predation risk.

anchor.quote: maximizing its net energy gain subject to the constraints of time and predation risk

facts.text: The forager is predicted to choose the diet or patch that yields the greatest energy return per unit of time.

anchor.quote: choose the diet or patch that yields the greatest energy return per unit of time

facts.text: Because time spent on one food item cannot be spent on another, foraging involves a tradeoff.

anchor.quote: time spent on one food item cannot be spent on another, foraging involves a tradeoff

misconceptions.text: Students assume a forager simply eats the largest prey, ignoring the time and risk constraints that shape the optimal diet.
misconceptions.corrective: Optimal foraging weighs energy gain against the time and risk costs, not prey size alone.

examples.text: A bird may skip large but hard-to-handle prey if smaller prey give more energy per minute.

mcBank.stem: Optimal foraging theory predicts a forager chooses the option that
options: maximizes energy gain per unit time
minimizes all movement
ignores predation risk
always eats the largest prey

mapping.objective: maximizing the forager's net energy gain
mapping.decision variables: the diet or patch the forager chooses
mapping.tradeoff: time spent on one food item cannot be spent on another

definition.text: Cellular respiration is a staged process that releases energy from glucose through an ordered sequence of glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.

anchor.quote: an ordered sequence: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation

facts.text: Each stage depends on the products of the previous one; the citric acid cycle uses the pyruvate produced by glycolysis.

anchor.quote: the citric acid cycle uses the pyruvate produced by glycolysis

facts.text: Blocking an earlier stage halts the later ones.

anchor.quote: Blocking an earlier stage halts the later ones

misconceptions.text: Students treat the stages of respiration as an arbitrary list, missing that each stage feeds the next.
misconceptions.corrective: The order is forced by dependency: later stages consume the products of earlier ones.

examples.text: A poison that blocks glycolysis starves the citric acid cycle of pyruvate.

mcBank.stem: Why must the stages of cellular respiration occur in order?
options: each stage uses the previous stage's products
the stages are fully independent
the order is purely conventional
later stages can run first

mapping.stages: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation
mapping.dependency: each stage uses the products of the previous stage
mapping.failure if skipped: blocking an earlier stage halts the later ones

definition.text: A population's size changes only through its rates: it grows by births and immigration and shrinks by deaths and emigration.

anchor.quote: A population's size changes only through its rates: it grows by births and immigration and shrinks by deaths and emigration

facts.text: When births and immigration exceed deaths and emigration the population grows, and when the rates are equal the size holds steady.

anchor.quote: when the rates are equal the size holds steady

facts.text: Logistic growth slows as the population nears the carrying capacity its environment can sustain.

anchor.quote: logistic growth slows as the population nears the carrying capacity its environment can sustain

misconceptions.text: Students expect the population size to jump the moment the birth rate rises, confusing the level (size) with the rate (births per year).
misconceptions.corrective: A flow change bends the trajectory of the level over time; it does not instantly reset the level.

examples.text: A pond stocked with fish: the number of fish rises gradually as births outpace deaths, not instantly when spawning increases.

mcBank.stem: A population's size stops changing when
options: the birth rate and immigration rate both fall to exactly zero
total additions equal total removals over the same period
the carrying capacity of the environment suddenly doubles
emigration alone exceeds the rate of immigration

definition.text: A bioindicator is a species or biological response used to measure the health of an ecosystem that cannot be assessed all at once.

anchor.quote: a species or biological response used to measure the health of an ecosystem that cannot be assessed all at once

facts.text: The presence of pollution-sensitive mayfly larvae indicates good water quality, while their absence signals degradation.

anchor.quote: indicates good water quality, while their absence signals degradation

facts.text: A bioindicator captures the conditions it is sensitive to and misses stressors it does not respond to.

anchor.quote: A bioindicator captures the conditions it is sensitive to and misses stressors it does not respond to

misconceptions.text: Students treat one indicator species as a full measure of ecosystem health, forgetting it misses stressors it is not sensitive to.
misconceptions.corrective: Hold the construct (ecosystem health) fixed and pair the indicator with others that capture different stressors.

examples.text: A stream with abundant mayfly larvae reads as healthy on that indicator, yet could still carry a heavy-metal load the larvae tolerate.

mcBank.stem: A single bioindicator species gives an incomplete picture of ecosystem health because
options: it misses stressors it is not sensitive to
all species respond identically to every kind of pollution there is
ecosystem health can instead be measured directly and instantly
indicator species are far too rare to ever be observed

mapping.what the measure captures: the conditions the species is sensitive to
mapping.what it misses: stressors the species does not respond to

definition.text: Where to draw the boundary of a species is a contested choice, because no single definition fits every case.

anchor.quote: where to draw the boundary of a species is a contested choice

facts.text: Drawing the species boundary determines which populations are counted as endangered and protected.

anchor.quote: it determines which populations are counted as endangered and protected

facts.text: Different species concepts include and exclude different organisms.

anchor.quote: Different species concepts include and exclude different organisms

misconceptions.text: Students treat a species as a fixed natural fact rather than a human-drawn boundary that different definitions place differently.
misconceptions.corrective: Sort the same organisms under two species concepts and ask which populations gain or lose protection.

examples.text: Two populations ranked as one species or two — depending on the concept used — can decide whether a rare population is legally protected.

mcBank.stem: Where to draw the boundary of a species matters because
options: it determines which populations are protected as endangered
the definition of a species is fixed and never debated anywhere
species boundaries carry no real-world consequences
every organism belongs to one obvious species

mapping.stake of the boundary: which populations count as endangered and protected
